Hello Doctor NerdLove,
Why does dating feel like one huge, never-ending performance review where I’m somehow expected to know what the evaluation criteria are without anyone actually telling me what they are?

I know that probably sounds especially ridiculous coming from someone with a degree in business management. And maybe some of this is just years of frustration talking. But seriously, how the hell can this whole process be this fucked up?

I’ve been trying to get into a relationship for years. And every once in a while, I think I’ve finally met someone where the interest seems mutual. We get along. There’s chemistry. We keep talking. Things seem to be going well and for once I think, Okay, maybe this is actually going somewhere.
And then suddenly there’s another hurdle.

Something I was apparently supposed to know already. Some unspoken expectation. Some invisible rule about how I was supposed to behave, what I was supposed to say, how quickly I was supposed to respond, how much interest I was supposed to show, or how much interest was apparently too much.
And if I don’t handle that particular situation exactly right, that’s it. I’m out.
Nobody gives you the fucking rubric afterward, either.

Dating starts feeling less like getting to know another person and more like applying for a job where nobody actually gives you the job description. The interview questions change halfway through. And then, when you don’t get hired, nobody will tell you why.
And the worst part is that it feels like other people don’t even have to play this game.

Maybe they won the genetic lottery. Maybe they happened to get some combination of looks, confidence, charm and social instincts that just works. Maybe they happened to be in the right place at the right time and met someone who liked them. Maybe it’s just blind fucking luck.
And sure, I can try to learn from what they have going for them.

I can work on my confidence. Try to be more charming. Pay attention to how they talk to people. Learn how they flirt. Put more effort into my appearance. Try to figure out what they’re doing differently and imitate it.
I’ve done a lot of that.
But somehow it never seems to get me the same results.

I can copy the behavior. I can try to develop the same qualities. I can follow the advice and use the techniques. But whatever combination of things makes it work for them just doesn’t seem to translate when I do it.
It’s like watching someone who knows exactly how to play an instrument, copying every movement of their hands, and somehow still producing a completely different fucking sound.
Whatever the reason, some people seem to be able to walk up to someone, say something stupid, laugh about it, and somehow end up having the time of their lives together.
Meanwhile, I’m over here trying to reverse-engineer the fucking software before I’m even allowed to run the program.

Because what’s the point of finally figuring out the rules if, by the time I meet someone new and try to actually use what I learned, I’m going to be judged against a completely different set of rules anyway?
Be more confident. Fine.
Don’t come on too strong. Okay.
Show interest. But not too much.
Take initiative. But don’t pressure her.
Be vulnerable. But don’t dump your problems on her.
Be yourself. But apparently not that version of yourself.

Before I dig into this letter, I want to point out that I cut nearly 1000 words just to get it to something a little more readable and frankly I could probably cut more to help distill it further to the meat of the problem. I realize that people’s situations can be complex and there’s often nuance and context involved, but there becomes a point where less is more and more can lead to intellectual and emotional detours and cul-de-sacs, rather than clarity.
So with that out of the way, let’s get to the meat of the matter: you’re frustrated, you aren’t sure what you’re doing wrong and in the attempt to figure out what you’re doing wrong, you’re inventing boogiemen to rail against and false comparisons to base your expectations on.

You can see this in your letter when you try to anticipate what I’m going to say and respond to that. You’re trying to forestall things that you think you already know are coming, but you really have no way of knowing. Maybe you’re right, maybe you’re not, but you are treating what you expect as having functionally already happened and responding to that instead of taking things as they come and responding then.

This is something that comes up a lot: people resorting to what they assume must be the case and treating it as fact. What’s fascinating, in a perverse sort of way, is how often this starts as a series of rhetorical flourishes – ways of trying to describe how something feels, before eventually crystalizing into “…that must be what’s wrong.” You say it enough times, it starts to make sense and your brain will backwards engineer that into belief that this is the problem. And that will, in turn, lead you to other, equally unhelpful conclusions. They’ll be conclusions that follow “logically” and reasonably, but they’re neither helpful nor are they true. They’re just going to compound the misery and throw more roadblocks in your path. Especially as it inevitably leads to increasingly polarized and catastrophic thinking and beliefs.

Everything you say about “what if someone better comes along” is precisely part of that, because you’re right, that’s not how relationships work, and that is something you have to unlearn. Nobody is in a relationship because they’re killing time until they can upgrade to a better model, they’re in a relationship with that person because they like that specific person.
Remember that last bit. Put a pin in it. It’s gonna be relevant in a few minutes.

So here’s the thing about dating: there are no “rules”, because dating is about how people feel. We try to apply rules to give structure and a sense of control to the process, to try to streamline what is honestly a clunky and inefficient process, but those “rules” are entirely made up and based on nothing more than societal expectations and vibes. Even the “rules” of courtship from when dating was more structured and social mores were more stringent were more about forcing specific outcomes and compliance with social expectations of behavior, not facilitating a better connection or more meaningful relationship. But at the end of the day, the rules are all made up and the points don’t mean anything, because feelings couldn’t give less of a fuck about your “rules”. At best, what you have are a series of best practices, things that are often broadly applicable for not making mistakes or avoiding unnecessary roadblocks, but do not and can not apply universally, 100% of the time.

The “rules” of dating have nothing to do with actual rules and far more with general society’s ideas of behavior. Dating culture is a prime example of this; even the dating culture between relatively comparable communities or countries – say, the US and the United Kingdom – can vary wildly.

The idea of “rules” are comforting because it implies structure, order and, more importantly, control. But rules can’t, by definition, account for what makes one person like another. There is no way to set up rules that will keep someone from deciding they’re not into another person, not because that person did anything wrong, but because lunch isn’t sitting well and it’s affecting their mood. Or because one person got cut off in traffic and the level of irritation has made them especially sensitive that day.

This is one of the reasons why I quote the philosopher Jean-Luc Picard so frequently: because you can follow “the rules” perfectly and do everything “right”, but the reason you two didn’t click has nothing to do with any of the rules.

This is also why there are people who don’t seem to follow “the rules” and succeed or who seem to have no problem meeting people. There’re so many things going on that you have not and cannot perceive that basing your assumption on what you do see is an exercise in folly. It’s not just “this person is hot, therefore they get to do what they please”, nor is it “the rules don’t exist for this person, but do for others”, it’s “this person is good at identifying folks they click with”. Or “this person is skilled at building connections with people because they grew up in a way that made it easier for them to form stable relationships”. Or even “this person got stupid lucky and you just happened to be there when they did.”

You, I might point out, also aren’t seeing what happened before after. You may see them laughing and having the time of their lives, but you’re not seeing the relationship when you’re not around. You’re not seeing that the person that gets picked up had a day that left them in the mood to meet someone

You’re not seeing whether the dates went well, whether one person is having regrets or the other person is starting to let their standards for behavior slip because they don’t feel like they need to put in effort. What you see is, at best, the tip of the metaphorical iceberg; the real action is what’s happening beneath the surface. The comparisons are, perhaps, somewhat inevitable, but they’re inaccurate and basing your expectations – for good or ill – on them are unhelpful at best and an active hindrance at best. Even if you’re looking at it as behavior to emulate, you’re doing so without the full picture, which means that the most you can really expect is a cargo-cult version of that behavior.
https://www.doctornerdlove.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/shutterstock_1721152858.jpg

It’s also why mimicry or imitation isn’t helping for its own sake. To use your metaphor, just because you can reproduce the motions of someone playing a violin, it doesn’t help if you don’t know what the notes are supposed to sound like or which strings produce which chords. Going through the motions without the understanding of the purpose of those motions or the results they’re meant to bring about isn’t going to help the way you hope, not teach you how to play violin without ever picking one up.

(Does this conflict with my “fake it ‘til you make it?” philosophy? No, not really, because the point of “fake it ‘til you make it” isn’t “imitate other people to be successful”, it’s “adopt the behaviors and practices of how you would act if you believed good things about yourself until you come to believe it for real.”)

This is the ultimate problem with the idea that there’re rules that you’re not following correctly or that you’re being judged on criteria that keeps changing. You’re missing the forest for the trees, because the problem isn’t that you’re not following the rules or etiquette or speaking the right shibboleth. Your attention is in the wrong places and it’s leading you down unhelpful paths.

I can already hear you saying “great, literally none of that helps me out of my situation, Doc”, but stick with me. The problem here isn’t that you’re not following the rules. The problem is very simple: you’re focused on the wrong things. When you strip it down to its bare essentials, what makes the difference between a good date or a bad one or a connection with a person vs. a rejection is just this: whether they like you and want to spend more time with you.

So the question you want to be asking yourself is: what are you doing to be more likeable? What is it that you can do to have a better time and facilitate the other person having a good time with you on dates? What can you cultivate in yourself that will make you someone people enjoy hanging out with and – importantly – are you choosing people that you would want to hang out with or not?

That last one is important; I’m a big believer that you shouldn’t try to date someone if you couldn’t be friends with them if sex or romance isn’t on the table. If the only reason why you would want to spend time with someone is because you find them attractive or want to date them, then the odds are good that this is someone you’re ultimately not that compatible with.

But that’s more of a secondary issue at the moment because I suspect the likeability is a bigger issue for you. Some of this is born out of the stress and trying to figure out what you’re doing wrong; I would be willing to bet you cash money that your last several dates were spent more in your head than in the moment. If you look back at them, can you honestly say that you were fully present and vibing with that person and trying to get to know them? Or were you splitting your attention between them and the meta-analysis of “how is this date going?” I can tell you from experience – both personal and professional ­– that the latter is a great way to end up with dates that you thought went well but never lead anywhere.

But another part is going to be in your overall mood and attitude. Your sign-off is a great example; I know it’s hyperbole for the sake of effect, but “I’ll find new and exciting reasons why I’ll get rejected” is the sort of jokey-joke that’s not actually a joke. It’s the vibe you’re putting out into the world and people are going to respond to it because I can promise you: you’re not that good of an actor or poker player. And that’s going to fuck with your ability to connect with people because that aspect is going to be coming through in the way you behave.

I’m going to ask you to do something, and I want you to try to do this exercise as sincerely and honestly as you can, with as little self-recrimination, blame or self-deprecation that you can. I want you to take how you feel – the things that you’re thinking, the ways that you’re behaving when you’re alone, the way that you’re feeling about yourself on a day-to-day basis – and ask yourself: would you want to date you? Rather: would you want to date someone who behaved, thought and felt like this? Would you find that overall attitude and behavior attractive? Would you be willing to overlook the ways that these internal beliefs influence their behavior? Or would you see someone with that attitude and behavior as someone you’d rather not spend time with?

If you are about to ask “Well how would I know that about them?” then you’re missing the point. You know. You may not know how you know but you know. Focusing on the how is, again, missing the forest for the trees because the problem is the way you feel and the attitude you’re carrying, not that you’re not good enough at concealing it.

The answer to this question is going to lead to a second question: which aspects of that person are the ones that would be the ones that are most likely to push you away from them? Which of those behaviors and attitudes are the ones you find the most significant and least appealing? Can you see how those might interfere with building a connection and a relationship with someone?

This is important because here’s a thing that gets lost in the mix: opposites don’t attract. We tend to like people who are like us and the more similar we are – especially in areas like values, personality, goals and ambitions – the more we tend to be drawn to them. So, the point of this experiment is that if you can see those aspects and how they might not appeal to you, you have a better grasp on how other people are going to feel about them.

Now the point isn’t to say “this is why you’re single: it’s because you suck.” It’s to see how you may be getting in your own way, so that you can start fixing those things. And one of the first things I think you need to do is to just take a break. It’s kind of like how if you’ve been beating your head against the wall forever and nothing is changing, the first step isn’t to change the angle or amount of force you’re generating with your neck, it’s to stop beating your head against things. Part of why you’re frustrated is that you’re doing the same things over and over again and it’s not working. Well… stop. Take a break. Step away for a little while and do other things that will let you take your focus elsewhere and give your batteries a chance to recharge and your nervous system to settle down.

Yeah, I know, it’s not what you want to hear and it’s the sort of thing that feels like it just prolongs the problem. But it’s a little like trying to run when you haven’t eaten properly in days; you’re not wanting to slow down to eat because you’re worried that it’ll delay your arrival, but not eating is fucking with your ability to run. The time it takes to sit, rest, recoup and get some proper nutrition in you is significantly shorter than how long it will take you to get where you’re going in the shape you’re in currently.

So it is with taking a break when you’re getting frustrated. The frustration is sapping your mental bandwidth, exacerbating your negative emotions and leading you to make mistakes. You’re like a poker player who’s gone on tiltand you need to break out of that state… which you can’t do by continuing to do the things that put you in tilt in the first place. As frustrating as it can be, you have to swallow the losses and step away from the table. Continuing as you are is just the sunk cost fallacy, where you’re investing more and more of yourself in hopes of making that initial investment pay off, even though no win could recoup everything that you’ve thrown into this by now. You have to be willing to say “I’ve lost enough time and energy to this and I need to stop, instead of losing more.”

Will it suck? Yeah. It’ll make you feel like a loser. You’ll want to beat yourself up for all the mistakes you made and all the things you should’ve done differently. And none of that is helpful. The best thing you can do is, in fact, be willing to forgive yourself instead. You made the best decisions you could at the time with the information you had, and it didn’t pan out the way you hoped. But now that you have more information, better information, you can make new, different and better choices in the future.
But a player on tilt first has to stop playing. You have to stop beating your head against the wall before you can figure out how to get around it. And then you have to recover.

Give yourself permission to take some time off from dating and just work on yourself a bit. Working on yourself, in this case, is going to look like doing the things that rest and relax your body and recharge your soul. It’s going to look like getting back in touch with things that you may have been putting off or putting aside that have importance and meaning to you – things that you love doing because they bring you fulfillment and satisfaction. It looks like reaching out to friends and spending more time with them, reminding yourself that there are people who love and care for you.

That, in turn, helps you put your focus and attention where it needs to be: not on trying to reverse engineer the “rules” that you’re not following or spending every date in a preemptive defensive crouch, but on having a good time. Not even thinking about will there be a second date, but just having a good time right now. In that moment. Getting to know that person, seeing what makes them tick and what makes them cool. And, importantly, taking them as individuals and not the latest representative of a collective that’s looking to reject you.

So take a step back. Push away from the table. It’s time for rest and recovery, then reconnection, then reconsideration. The rest is to recoup your energy, the recovery to let the scrapes and cuts and bruises to your ego to heal. The reconnection helps you remember the relationships you already have and how those came to be, while you reconsider your approach and your relationship to yourself.
Then, in the future, when you’re ready to get back in, be in the moment. Focus precisely on what you say you want: Okay, we like each other. We get along. Let’s see what we can build together.
Start by being likeable and finding people you like. See if you enjoy spending time with them and help them enjoy their time with you. And then you’ll see where things go from there.

There’s no competition, and women aren’t looking to weed you out. You’re not competing with other people, you’re competing with Netflix. You’re competing with a night playing board games with friends. You’re competing with how frustrating dating can be.

Just as importantly, women are on your side in this. If she’s on a date with you, that’s because at some level, she’s hoping that this may be the first of the last dates she ever has to go on. That’s part of what you’re collaborating on here.

Yeah, there will still be rejection, because everyone gets rejected. Nobody is immune, nobody goes 5 for 5. Most of those rejections will have nothing to do with you and everything to do with bad luck and bad timing. So you learn to take those in stride, realize that it’s not about you and move forward.
Otherwise, you’re just going to end up in the same place you were before.
Good luck.

They’re just going to compound the misery and throw more roadblocks in your path. Especially as it inevitably leads to increasingly polarized and catastrophic thinking and beliefs.

Everything you say about “what if someone better comes along” is precisely part of that, because you’re right, that’s not how relationships work, and that is something you have to unlearn. Nobody is in a relationship because they’re killing time until they can upgrade to a better model, they’re in a relationship with that person because they like that specific person.

Remember that last bit. Put a pin in it. It’s gonna be relevant in a few minutes.

So here’s the thing about dating: there are no “rules”, because dating is about how people feel. We try to apply rules to give structure and a sense of control to the process, to try to streamline what is honestly a clunky and inefficient process, but those “rules” are entirely made up and based on nothing more than societal expectations and vibes. Even the “rules” of courtship from when dating was more structured and social mores were more stringent were more about forcing specific outcomes and compliance with social expectations of behavior, not facilitating a better connection or more meaningful relationship. But at the end of the day, the rules are all made up and the points don’t mean anything, because feelings couldn’t give less of a fuck about your “rules”. At best, what you have are a series of best practices, things that are often broadly applicable for not making mistakes or avoiding unnecessary roadblocks, but do not and can not apply universally, 100% of the time.

The “rules” of dating have nothing to do with actual rules and far more with general society’s ideas of behavior. Dating culture is a prime example of this; even the dating culture between relatively comparable communities or countries – say, the US and the United Kingdom – can vary wildly.

The idea of “rules” are comforting because it implies structure, order and, more importantly, control. But rules can’t, by definition, account for what makes one person like another. There is no way to set up rules that will keep someone from deciding they’re not into another person, not because that person did anything wrong, but because lunch isn’t sitting well and it’s affecting their mood. Or because one person got cut off in traffic and the level of irritation has made them especially sensitive that day.

This is one of the reasons why I quote the philosopher Jean-Luc Picard so frequently: because you can follow “the rules” perfectly and do everything “right”, but the reason you two didn’t click has nothing to do with any of the rules.

This is also why there are people who don’t seem to follow “the rules” and succeed or who seem to have no problem meeting people. There’re so many things going on that you have not and cannot perceive that basing your assumption on what you do see is an exercise in folly. It’s not just “this person is hot, therefore they get to do what they please”, nor is it “the rules don’t exist for this person, but do for others”, it’s “this person is good at identifying folks they click with”. Or “this person is skilled at building connections with people because they grew up in a way that made it easier for them to form stable relationships”. Or even “this person got stupid lucky and you just happened to be there when they did.”

You, I might point out, also aren’t seeing what happened before after. You may see them laughing and having the time of their lives, but you’re not seeing the relationship when you’re not around. You’re not seeing that the person that gets picked up had a day that left them in the mood to meet someone

You’re not seeing whether the dates went well, whether one person is having regrets or the other person is starting to let their standards for behavior slip because they don’t feel like they need to put in effort. What you see is, at best, the tip of the metaphorical iceberg; the real action is what’s happening beneath the surface. The comparisons are, perhaps, somewhat inevitable, but they’re inaccurate and basing your expectations – for good or ill – on them are unhelpful at best and an active hindrance at best. Even if you’re looking at it as behavior to emulate, you’re doing so without the full picture, which means that the most you can really expect is a cargo-cult version of that behavior.

It’s also why mimicry or imitation isn’t helping for its own sake. To use your metaphor, just because you can reproduce the motions of someone playing a violin, it doesn’t help if you don’t know what the notes are supposed to sound like or which strings produce which chords. Going through the motions without the understanding of the purpose of those motions or the results they’re meant to bring about isn’t going to help the way you hope, not teach you how to play violin without ever picking one up.

(Does this conflict with my “fake it ‘til you make it?” philosophy? No, not really, because the point of “fake it ‘til you make it” isn’t “imitate other people to be successful”, it’s “adopt the behaviors and practices of how you would act if you believed good things about yourself until you come to believe it for real.”)

This is the ultimate problem with the idea that there’re rules that you’re not following correctly or that you’re being judged on criteria that keeps changing. You’re missing the forest for the trees, because the problem isn’t that you’re not following the rules or etiquette or speaking the right shibboleth. Your attention is in the wrong places and it’s leading you down unhelpful paths.

I can already hear you saying “great, literally none of that helps me out of my situation, Doc”, but stick with me. The problem here isn’t that you’re not following the rules. The problem is very simple: you’re focused on the wrong things. When you strip it down to its bare essentials, what makes the difference between a good date or a bad one or a connection with a person vs. a rejection is just this: whether they like you and want to spend more time with you.

So the question you want to be asking yourself is: what are you doing to be more likeable? What is it that you can do to have a better time and facilitate the other person having a good time with you on dates? What can you cultivate in yourself that will make you someone people enjoy hanging out with and – importantly – are you choosing people that you would want to hang out with or not?

That last one is important; I’m a big believer that you shouldn’t try to date someone if you couldn’t be friends with them if sex or romance isn’t on the table. If the only reason why you would want to spend time with someone is because you find them attractive or want to date them, then the odds are good that this is someone you’re ultimately not that compatible with.

But that’s more of a secondary issue at the moment because I suspect the likeability is a bigger issue for you. Some of this is born out of the stress and trying to figure out what you’re doing wrong; I would be willing to bet you cash money that your last several dates were spent more in your head than in the moment. If you look back at them, can you honestly say that you were fully present and vibing with that person and trying to get to know them? Or were you splitting your attention between them and the meta-analysis of “how is this date going?” I can tell you from experience – both personal and professional ­– that the latter is a great way to end up with dates that you thought went well but never lead anywhere.

But another part is going to be in your overall mood and attitude. Your sign-off is a great example; I know it’s hyperbole for the sake of effect, but “I’ll find new and exciting reasons why I’ll get rejected” is the sort of jokey-joke that’s not actually a joke. It’s the vibe you’re putting out into the world and people are going to respond to it because I can promise you: you’re not that good of an actor or poker player. And that’s going to fuck with your ability to connect with people because that aspect is going to be coming through in the way you behave.

I’m going to ask you to do something, and I want you to try to do this exercise as sincerely and honestly as you can, with as little self-recrimination, blame or self-deprecation that you can. I want you to take how you feel – the things that you’re thinking, the ways that you’re behaving when you’re alone, the way that you’re feeling about yourself on a day-to-day basis – and ask yourself: would you want to date you? Rather: would you want to date someone who behaved, thought and felt like this? Would you find that overall attitude and behavior attractive? Would you be willing to overlook the ways that these internal beliefs influence their behavior? Or would you see someone with that attitude and behavior as someone you’d rather not spend time with?

If you are about to ask “Well how would I know that about them?” then you’re missing the point. You know. You may not know how you know but you know. Focusing on the how is, again, missing the forest for the trees because the problem is the way you feel and the attitude you’re carrying, not that you’re not good enough at concealing it.

The answer to this question is going to lead to a second question: which aspects of that person are the ones that would be the ones that are most likely to push you away from them? Which of those behaviors and attitudes are the ones you find the most significant and least appealing? Can you see how those might interfere with building a connection and a relationship with someone?

This is important because here’s a thing that gets lost in the mix: opposites don’t attract. We tend to like people who are like us and the more similar we are – especially in areas like values, personality, goals and ambitions – the more we tend to be drawn to them. So, the point of this experiment is that if you can see those aspects and how they might not appeal to you, you have a better grasp on how other people are going to feel about them.

Now the point isn’t to say “this is why you’re single: it’s because you suck.” It’s to see how you may be getting in your own way, so that you can start fixing those things. And one of the first things I think you need to do is to just take a break. It’s kind of like how if you’ve been beating your head against the wall forever and nothing is changing, the first step isn’t to change the angle or amount of force you’re generating with your neck, it’s to stop beating your head against things. Part of why you’re frustrated is that you’re doing the same things over and over again and it’s not working. Well… stop. Take a break. Step away for a little while and do other things that will let you take your focus elsewhere and give your batteries a chance to recharge and your nervous system to settle down.

Yeah, I know, it’s not what you want to hear and it’s the sort of thing that feels like it just prolongs the problem. But it’s a little like trying to run when you haven’t eaten properly in days; you’re not wanting to slow down to eat because you’re worried that it’ll delay your arrival, but not eating is fucking with your ability to run. The time it takes to sit, rest, recoup and get some proper nutrition in you is significantly shorter than how long it will take you to get where you’re going in the shape you’re in currently.

So it is with taking a break when you’re getting frustrated. The frustration is sapping your mental bandwidth, exacerbating your negative emotions and leading you to make mistakes. You’re like a poker player who’s gone on tiltand you need to break out of that state… which you can’t do by continuing to do the things that put you in tilt in the first place. As frustrating as it can be, you have to swallow the losses and step away from the table. Continuing as you are is just the sunk cost fallacy, where you’re investing more and more of yourself in hopes of making that initial investment pay off, even though no win could recoup everything that you’ve thrown into this by now. You have to be willing to say “I’ve lost enough time and energy to this and I need to stop, instead of losing more.”

Will it suck? Yeah. It’ll make you feel like a loser. You’ll want to beat yourself up for all the mistakes you made and all the things you should’ve done differently. And none of that is helpful. The best thing you can do is, in fact, be willing to forgive yourself instead. You made the best decisions you could at the time with the information you had, and it didn’t pan out the way you hoped. But now that you have more information, better information, you can make new, different and better choices in the future.

But a player on tilt first has to stop playing. You have to stop beating your head against the wall before you can figure out how to get around it. And then you have to recover.

Give yourself permission to take some time off from dating and just work on yourself a bit. Working on yourself, in this case, is going to look like doing the things that rest and relax your body and recharge your soul. It’s going to look like getting back in touch with things that you may have been putting off or putting aside that have importance and meaning to you – things that you love doing because they bring you fulfillment and satisfaction. It looks like reaching out to friends and spending more time with them, reminding yourself that there are people who love and care for you.

That, in turn, helps you put your focus and attention where it needs to be: not on trying to reverse engineer the “rules” that you’re not following or spending every date in a preemptive defensive crouch, but on having a good time. Not even thinking about will there be a second date, but just having a good time right now. In that moment. Getting to know that person, seeing what makes them tick and what makes them cool. And, importantly, taking them as individuals and not the latest representative of a collective that’s looking to reject you.

So take a step back. Push away from the table. It’s time for rest and recovery, then reconnection, then reconsideration. The rest is to recoup your energy, the recovery to let the scrapes and cuts and bruises to your ego to heal. The reconnection helps you remember the relationships you already have and how those came to be, while you reconsider your approach and your relationship to yourself.

Then, in the future, when you’re ready to get back in, be in the moment. Focus precisely on what you say you want: Okay, we like each other. We get along. Let’s see what we can build together.

Start by being likeable and finding people you like. See if you enjoy spending time with them and help them enjoy their time with you. And then you’ll see where things go from there.

There’s no competition, and women aren’t looking to weed you out. You’re not competing with other people, you’re competing with Netflix. You’re competing with a night playing board games with friends. You’re competing with how frustrating dating can be.

Just as importantly, women are on your side in this. If she’s on a date with you, that’s because at some level, she’s hoping that this may be the first of the last dates she ever has to go on. That’s part of what you’re collaborating on here.

Yeah, there will still be rejection, because everyone gets rejected. Nobody is immune, nobody goes 5 for 5. Most of those rejections will have nothing to do with you and everything to do with bad luck and bad timing. So you learn to take those in stride, realize that it’s not about you and move forward.

Otherwise, you’re just going to end up in the same place you were before.

Good luck.
